title: The real presence (CCC 1373–1381)
hook: Christ present in the word, the priest, the people, and above all under the species

segments.voice: Yesterday, sacrifice and memorial, and the word anamnesis. Your line was present, not repeated. What did you make present for someone you love? Day one thousand ninety-nine.

A man in a work jacket comes in out of the rain, dips his fingers in the holy water, walks halfway down the aisle, and stops. His right knee goes down to the floor for a second, his eyes on a small gold box at the front with a lamp burning beside it. Then he stands, slides into a pew, and sits. He didn't kneel to the altar, or to the crowd, or to the building. He knelt toward that box. Why? Because of what the Church teaches is kept inside it. Today's word is the reason for that knee.
screen: `IN FROM THE RAIN.` → `ONE KNEE TO THE FLOOR.` → `TOWARD A SMALL GOLD BOX.`

segments.voice: The Catechism starts wide. Christ is present to his Church in many ways. In his word. In the Church's prayer, because he said, in the Douay-Rheims, "where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." In the poor, the sick, the imprisoned. In the sacraments. In the sacrifice of the Mass, and in the person of the priest. But above all, the Catechism says, he is present under the Eucharistic species, the bread and wine. That presence it calls unique. Quoting the Council of Trent, it says the body and blood of Christ, with his soul and divinity, the whole Christ, are contained in the sacrament truly, really, and substantially. Three words, each shutting a door. Truly: not as a picture. Really: not only in the mind of the believer. Substantially: in what the bread and wine are, not just how they look. The Church calls this change transubstantiation. The Catechism says the presence begins at the consecration and lasts as long as the species do, and that Christ is whole and entire in each of them and in every part. Behind it all is Jesus's own line in John's Gospel: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." Then comes the practical part. Because of this, the Catechism says, the Church shows adoration by genuflecting or bowing deeply, and keeps the Eucharist in the tabernacle, for the sick and for prayer. And it's honest about the limit. Quoting Thomas Aquinas, it says this presence can't be grasped by the senses, only by faith. That's the knee in the aisle.
screen: `MANY WAYS PRESENT.` · `ABOVE ALL, UNDER BREAD AND WINE.` · `TRULY, REALLY, SUBSTANTIALLY.` · `KNEELING, AND KEPT FOR PRAYER.` · then, large: `MY FLESH IS MEAT INDEED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: genuflect with attention. If you're near a church, go in, find the tabernacle with its lamp, and bend one knee slowly, as if it's the first time. If not, stand wherever you are and do it there, or simply bow your head, if your knees won't cooperate. The Catechism names a deep bow too. Then sit, and breathe. Say the three words to yourself, one per breath: truly. Really. Substantially. If you pray, you can stay in adoration until the bell. If you don't, just notice what it's like to kneel to something. The bell holds the time.
Real presence. Christ present in many ways, and above all under the bread and wine: truly, really, substantially. Today's word.

Your line: truly, really, substantially. This week went from many rites to baptism, confirmation, and the Eucharist's names, sacrifice and presence. Today, the next time you pass a church, slow down for one breath as you go by. Day one thousand ninety-nine.

howItsDone: In Latin-rite churches people customarily genuflect toward the tabernacle when entering or leaving a pew, and some parishes hold Eucharistic adoration, with the host displayed in a monstrance for silent prayer.

fork.setup: you're walking into a church toward a pew, but your knee won't bend. what does the Catechism name as a sign of adoration?
options: no sign at all is expected.
fork.reveal: the Catechism names both genuflecting and bowing deeply as signs of adoration.

'truly, really, and substantially' is the carry and Trent's phrase via CCC 1374; spoken without quotation marks and cited as paraphrase. The glosses 'not as a picture / not only in the mind / in what the bread and wine are' are the writer's explanation; Keeper should confirm.
Hook is a scene; the tabernacle described as 'a small gold box' varies by church.
No comparison with other churches' understanding of the Eucharist was included; Keeper may want a line on differing Christian views.
